misconception_description: Student believes that conditional statements, i.e., Python statements that evaluate to either True or False, must be explicitly compared to True or False to be used in conditionals.

solutions.generated_code:
program DamagePokemon
kamus
  attackerTipe, defenderTipe : string
  attackerLevel, defenderLevel : integer
  efektivitas : real
  selisihLevel, damage : integer
algoritma
  input(attackerTipe, attackerLevel)
  input(defenderTipe, defenderLevel)
  if (attackerTipe == defenderTipe) == true then
    efektivitas <- 1
  else if (attackerTipe == "fire" and defenderTipe == "grass") == true then
    efektivitas <- 2
  else if (attackerTipe == "grass" and defenderTipe == "water") == true then
    efektivitas <- 2
  else if (attackerTipe == "water" and defenderTipe == "fire") == true then
    efektivitas <- 2
  else
    efektivitas <- 0.5
  endif
  selisihLevel <- attackerLevel - defenderLevel
  damage <- bulat(((2 * attackerLevel) / 5 + 2) * (attackerLevel / defenderLevel) * efektivitas * selisihLevel / 10)
  if damage < 1 then
    damage <- 1
  endif
  output(damage)
endprogram

metadata.modification_notes: The student believes that all conditional expressions must be explicitly compared to True or False to be used in if/elif statements. Each condition like `attacker_type == defender_type` already evaluates to a Boolean value, but the student adds `== True` to make it explicit. This is redundant but does not affect the correctness of the code - the logic remains identical and all test cases will pass. The student genuinely believes this explicit comparison is the proper way to write conditional statements in Python.
